categories.name: Access control and privilege
categories.description: Privileged state changes or fund movements reachable by callers who should not have that power.
categories.question: The source file in `source` contains an access-control vulnerability: a function that moves funds, mints or burns tokens, changes critical parameters, or grants roles can be called by an unauthorized address, because an authorization check is missing, wrong, or bypassable, or roles are assigned incorrectly. The flaw lets an attacker steal or freeze assets or take over the protocol. Centralization risk from an honest, correctly-gated admin does not count.

subcategories.name: Missing authorization on privileged function
subcategories.description: External/public function that changes critical state or moves funds has no caller check.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a missing-authorization bug: an external or public function that transfers funds, mints, burns, sets critical parameters, changes owners/roles, or withdraws protocol assets has no effective caller restriction (no modifier, require, or role check), so any address can call it and steal funds or seize control.
code_patterns: external/public setter or withdraw/mint/sweep with no onlyOwner/onlyRole/require(msg.sender==...)
internal-intended helper accidentally declared public/external
callback entry point (e.g. onFlashLoan, uniswapV3SwapCallback) that does not verify msg.sender or initiator
emergency/rescue function without access modifier

subcategories.name: Incorrect authorization logic
subcategories.description: An authorization check exists but is wrong: inverted, wrong variable, wrong role, or OR instead of AND.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a flawed authorization check: a guard on a privileged function checks the wrong address, wrong role, wrong mapping key, uses || where && is required, is inverted, or is only applied on some code paths, so an unauthorized caller passes the check and can perform the privileged action to steal funds or change critical state.
code_patterns: require(msg.sender == owner || ...) with an attacker-satisfiable second clause
modifier checks a parameter address instead of msg.sender
role check against wrong role constant
check applied in one overload/entry point but not a sibling that reaches the same state

subcategories.name: Acting on behalf of arbitrary accounts
subcategories.description: Function takes an address or id selecting another party's funds or position and acts on it without verifying the caller owns it or is approved.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains an on-behalf-of authorization bug: a function takes a parameter that selects another party's funds or position (an owner, account, or `from` address, or the id of a pool, vault, position, loan, order, or deposit) and spends, withdraws, transfers, lends from, borrows against, or reassigns those funds or that position without checking that msg.sender is its owner or an approved delegate, so an attacker can use or drain other users' approved tokens, balances, or positions.
code_patterns: transferFrom(from, ...) where `from` is a caller-supplied parameter and msg.sender is never compared to it
withdraw(owner, receiver, amount) with no allowance or approval check for msg.sender
function that debits balances[id] or pools[id] for a caller-supplied id without require(ownerOf[id] == msg.sender)
router or zap that pulls funds from a user-specified address
operator or delegate mapping that exists but is never consulted

subcategories.name: Role and ownership management flaw
subcategories.description: Role grant/revoke, ownership transfer, or admin-role hierarchy lets roles be escalated or lost.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a role-management bug: role granting, revocation, or ownership transfer logic lets an unprivileged or lower-privileged account grant itself a higher role, prevents revocation of a compromised role, or transfers ownership to an unverified address in a way that lets an attacker gain control of privileged functions.
code_patterns: custom grantRole without admin-role check
role admin set to a role that anyone can hold
ownership set in a callable function other than constructor/initializer

categories.name: Cross-chain, bridge, and L2 messaging
categories.description: Message passing between chains or layers where sender, payload, or delivery is not validated.
categories.question: The source file in `source` contains a cross-chain messaging vulnerability: a bridge, messaging receiver, or L1/L2 integration accepts messages without verifying the source chain, source sender, endpoint caller, or proof, allows replay, or mishandles failed or reordered delivery, so an attacker can mint unbacked tokens, release escrowed funds, or permanently lock bridged assets.

subcategories.name: Unverified message sender or source chain
subcategories.description: Receiver does not check the calling endpoint, the origin chain, or the origin sender.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains an unverified-message bug: a cross-chain receive handler (lzReceive, ccipReceive, receiveWormholeMessages, xReceive, onMessage, L2 bridge callbacks) does not verify that msg.sender is the trusted endpoint and that the source chain and source sender are trusted, so an attacker can send forged messages that mint or release funds.
code_patterns: lzReceive without msg.sender == endpoint check
no trusted remote / peer mapping check
sourceChainSelector ignored
L2 xDomainMessageSender not verified

subcategories.name: Message replay or ordering flaw
subcategories.description: Messages can be processed twice, or out of order in a way that breaks state.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a message replay or ordering bug: inbound cross-chain messages or withdrawal proofs are not marked as processed before execution, the processed key omits chain or nonce, or out-of-order delivery breaks accounting, so an attacker can execute the same transfer twice or corrupt bridged balances.
code_patterns: processed[messageHash] set after external calls or not at all
message id omitting source chain
nonce ordering assumed on unordered channel
retry function re-executing successful messages

subcategories.name: Proof or root validation flaw
subcategories.description: Merkle proofs, state roots, or validator signatures validated insufficiently.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a proof-validation bug: bridge or messaging code accepts Merkle proofs, state roots, or validator/guardian signatures with a zero or default trusted root, insufficient threshold, duplicate signers, or unchecked leaf/node domain separation, letting an attacker forge withdrawals and steal escrowed funds.
code_patterns: acceptableRoot[0] == true or default root trusted
duplicate signer not rejected in threshold check
leaf and internal node hashed identically (second preimage)
validator set update without quorum

subcategories.name: Failed message handling locks funds
subcategories.description: Failed or reverted delivery leaves funds stuck with no retry or refund path.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a failed-message fund lock: when a cross-chain message fails on the destination (revert, insufficient gas, paused receiver, unsupported token), the source side has already burned or escrowed funds and there is no retry, refund, or recovery path, or an attacker can force the failure, permanently locking user funds.
code_patterns: burn on source before destination success is confirmed
gas limit for destination execution user-set without minimum
blocking channel where one failed message halts all subsequent ones
no refund address or retry mechanism

subcategories.name: L2 and chain-specific assumptions
subcategories.description: Assumptions about block.number, sequencer, address aliasing, PUSH0, or gas that break on L2s/alt-EVMs.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains an L2 or chain-specific assumption bug: the file relies on block.number timing, msg.sender equality across L1/L2 without address aliasing, sequencer liveness, or opcodes/precompiles not available on its deployment chain, so on the target chain an attacker can bypass time locks, impersonate cross-domain senders, or cause funds to be locked.
code_patterns: block.number used as time on Arbitrum/Optimism
L1 contract address compared on L2 without aliasing
no sequencer-down grace period for liquidations
hardcoded chain-specific addresses deployed multichain

categories.name: External calls and token integration
categories.description: Unsafe assumptions about external contracts and tokens: return values, fee-on-transfer, rebasing, approvals, arbitrary targets.
categories.question: The source file in `source` contains an external-call or token-integration vulnerability: the file makes external calls or token transfers without checking success, assumes standard ERC20 behaviour for tokens that deviate (fee-on-transfer, rebasing, no return value, blocklists, approval quirks), or lets callers choose arbitrary call targets or calldata, so an attacker can steal approved funds, credit themselves with tokens never received, or lock funds.
sources: Trail of Bits: token integration checklist

subcategories.name: Unchecked call or transfer return value
subcategories.description: Low-level call or ERC20 transfer/transferFrom/approve result ignored.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains an unchecked-return-value bug: the file ignores the boolean result of a low-level call/send, or calls ERC20 transfer/transferFrom/approve directly instead of SafeERC20 on tokens that return false instead of reverting, so failed transfers are treated as successful and users are credited or paid without funds moving.
code_patterns: token.transfer(to, amt); without require/SafeERC20
(bool ok, ) = to.call{value:v}(""); ok unused
send() result ignored
approve on USDT-style tokens without return value decoding

subcategories.name: Fee-on-transfer or rebasing tokens
subcategories.description: Accounting assumes received amount equals requested amount and balances are static.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a non-standard token accounting bug: the file credits the requested amount rather than the balance delta received, or caches token balances, while supporting arbitrary tokens that may charge transfer fees or rebase, so users are over-credited, later withdrawals fail, or depositors steal from each other.
code_patterns: deposit(amount) credits amount after transferFrom without balance-before/after
stETH/aTokens/AMPL-style balances cached in storage
whitelist absent for arbitrary ERC20 support

subcategories.name: Arbitrary call target or calldata
subcategories.description: User-supplied target/calldata executed from a contract holding approvals or funds.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains an arbitrary-external-call bug: the file executes a low-level call with a caller-supplied target address and/or calldata from a contract that holds tokens or user approvals, so an attacker can make it call `token.transferFrom(victim, attacker, ...)` or `approve`, stealing funds.
code_patterns: target.call(data) with target and data from params
swap aggregator router address not whitelisted
multicall/execute forwarding arbitrary calls
callback data decoded into an arbitrary call

subcategories.name: Approval handling flaw
subcategories.description: Leftover approvals, non-zero-to-non-zero approve reverts, or infinite approvals to untrusted spenders.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains an approval-handling bug: the contract leaves unused allowances to external routers that can later be spent, calls approve from non-zero to non-zero on tokens that revert on it (USDT), or grants unlimited approvals to user-controlled or upgradeable spenders, enabling theft of the contract's tokens or permanently blocking operations.
code_patterns: approve(router, amount) with no reset after partial use
approve(x, n) without first approving 0 for USDT
type(uint256).max approval to user-provided address
safeApprove from non-zero allowance

subcategories.name: Wrong assumption about integrated protocol
subcategories.description: Misusing an integrated protocol's API: return units, revert semantics, pausing, or state.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains an integration-assumption bug: the file calls an external protocol (AMM, lending market, staking contract, vault, oracle) assuming return units, revert behaviour, withdrawal availability, slippage behaviour, or paused state that the protocol does not guarantee, so funds are mispriced, stuck, or stolen when the integration behaves differently.
code_patterns: assuming ERC4626 withdraw returns shares when it returns assets (or vice versa)
ignoring external pause/withdraw limits
using returned value from a function that returns nothing meaningful
hardcoded pool fee tier or path

subcategories.name: ETH transfer and receive issues
subcategories.description: transfer/send gas stipend, missing receive, stuck msg.value, or refunds to contracts.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains an ETH-handling bug: the file sends ETH with `transfer`/`send` (2300 gas) to recipients that may be contracts, has payable functions that accept msg.value but never account for or refund it, or lacks a way to withdraw ETH it receives, so user ETH becomes permanently locked or payments fail.
code_patterns: payable function with msg.value never used
payable(x).transfer to multisig/contract wallets
receive() present with no withdrawal path
msg.value reused inside a loop or multicall

categories.name: Business logic, input validation, and state machine
categories.description: Protocol rules implemented incorrectly: missing validation, broken state transitions, wrong ordering, or violated invariants.
categories.question: The source file in `source` contains a business-logic vulnerability: the protocol's intended rules are implemented incorrectly, such as missing validation of user-supplied parameters, state transitions allowed out of order or repeatedly, time/deadline checks that are wrong, or a core invariant (solvency, collateralization, supply caps) that can be violated, letting an attacker extract value, bypass restrictions, or corrupt protocol state. View or pure functions that change no state do not count, unless state-changing code in the file uses their result.

subcategories.name: Missing input validation
subcategories.description: User parameters (addresses, amounts, ids, arrays) accepted without bounds or sanity checks.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a missing-input-validation bug: a function accepts caller-supplied addresses, amounts, ids, pool/market identifiers, or arrays without checking they are valid (non-zero, whitelisted, in range, matching lengths, existing), and an attacker can pass a fake pool/token/market or out-of-range value to steal funds or corrupt state.
code_patterns: market/pool/token address param not checked against registry
arrays of different lengths used in lockstep
amount == 0 or id not existing accepted
user-supplied path/route not validated

subcategories.name: Invalid state transition
subcategories.description: Actions allowed in the wrong lifecycle state or repeated when they must be one-shot.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains an invalid-state-transition bug: a lifecycle action (claim, finalize, settle, cancel, execute, redeem, close) can be performed in the wrong state, more than once, or after a conflicting action, because status flags are missing, checked incorrectly, or set in the wrong place, letting an attacker double-claim or withdraw funds they are not owed.
code_patterns: claimed flag checked but never set
status enum not checked in execute/cancel
cancel after partial fill refunds full amount

subcategories.name: Timing, lock, and deadline logic
subcategories.description: Lockups, vesting, cooldowns, epochs, or deadlines computed or enforced incorrectly.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a timing-logic bug: lock periods, vesting schedules, cooldowns, epochs, auctions, or deadlines are computed or compared incorrectly (off-by-one, < vs <=, reset or bypassed by transfer or re-deposit, wrong unit), so users can withdraw early, claim unvested tokens, or skip required waiting periods to extract value.
code_patterns: lock end not reset/extended on additional deposit
cooldown bypass via transfer to fresh address
epoch boundary off-by-one
vesting claimable computed from start not last claim

subcategories.name: Solvency or core invariant violation
subcategories.description: Operations that can leave the protocol undercollateralized or break supply/backing invariants.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a solvency-invariant bug: some sequence of user actions (borrow, withdraw, transfer collateral, redeem, mint) is not checked against the protocol's core invariant (health factor, collateral ratio, backing, supply cap), so a user can leave a position undercollateralized or mint unbacked tokens, leaving the protocol insolvent.
code_patterns: health check performed before rather than after state change
collateral transfer/withdraw path skipping health check
supply cap checked on deposit but not on mint
isolated vs cross-margin checks inconsistent

subcategories.name: Self-referential or identical-parameter edge case
subcategories.description: Same address/id passed twice (from == to, tokenA == tokenB, self-liquidation) breaks logic.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains an identical-parameter edge-case bug: logic mis-handles cases where two parameters are equal (from == to, sender == receiver, tokenIn == tokenOut, same id twice in an array, borrower == liquidator), such as reading a balance before and writing both sides, so an attacker can duplicate balances, rewards, or collateral.

categories.name: Denial of service and griefing
categories.description: Ways an attacker can block operations or permanently lock funds, even without profit.
categories.question: The source file in `source` contains a denial-of-service or griefing vulnerability: an attacker can make a critical function (withdraw, liquidate, claim, settle, upgrade) revert or become unusable, for example through unbounded loops, a reverting recipient, forced state changes, dust positions, or front-running a one-time action, temporarily or permanently freezing user or protocol funds.

subcategories.name: Unbounded loop gas exhaustion
subcategories.description: Loops over user-growable arrays or mappings that can exceed the block gas limit.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains an unbounded-loop DoS bug: a critical function iterates over an array or list that any user can grow cheaply (deposits, positions, holders, queue entries, reward tokens) with no bound or pagination, so an attacker can make it exceed the block gas limit and permanently block withdrawals, liquidations, or distributions.
code_patterns: for (i < users.length) where anyone can push
withdrawal queue processed fully in one call
reward tokens list extendable without cap
deleting from array by linear search

subcategories.description: A single failing external call (blocklisted token, reverting receiver) blocks a batch or a critical path.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a revert-based DoS bug: a critical path or batch loop performs push-style ETH or token transfers or calls to user-controlled addresses where one reverting recipient (contract without receive, blocklisted USDC/USDT address, malicious hook) makes the whole operation revert, blocking others' withdrawals, auctions, or liquidations.

refund to previous highest bidder in bid()

categories.name: Front-running, MEV, and randomness
categories.description: Transaction-ordering dependence, missing slippage/deadline protection, and predictable randomness.
categories.question: The source file in `source` contains a transaction-ordering or MEV vulnerability: the outcome of a user or protocol transaction depends on mempool ordering and lacks slippage limits, deadlines, commit-reveal, or unpredictable randomness, so a searcher or validator can sandwich, front-run, or back-run it, or predict/steer random outcomes, to steal value from users or the protocol.

subcategories.name: Front-runnable state change or claim
subcategories.description: A user's outcome depends on state another party can change or claim first, and the user cannot bound it.
subcategories.question: The source file in `source` contains a transaction-ordering bug in which a user cannot bound what another party does first. Either (a) a function executes a user's action (borrow, fill, buy, deposit) against a pool, order, offer, or listing owned by another user and applies that owner's current terms (interest rate, fee, price, loan ratio, or duration), which the owner can change at any time, without letting the user pass a limit or expected value for those terms, so the owner can change them just before the user's transaction lands; or (b) a transaction reveals information or claims a first-come benefit (a solution, bounty, reward notification, or arbitrage opportunity) without commit-reveal or sender binding, so an observer can copy or front-run it. Either way the other party takes value from the user. Parameter changes by a trusted admin do not count.
code_patterns: borrow, deposit, or buy function that copies an interest rate, fee, price, or duration from a record its owner can change at any time, with no max-rate, max-fee, or expected-value parameter
pool or order owner can update its rate, fee, or duration in the same block that a user's borrow, fill, or buy against it executes
claim(solution) without commit-reveal
notifyRewardAmount front-runnable by deposit-then-withdraw

blockhash(block.number - 1) as seed

VRF request re-rollable or fulfillment revertible
